breaking.bfsi_impact: A major South Korean crypto exchange has exposed highly sensitive customer data — including passwords, resident registration numbers, bank account numbers and wallet addresses — through its customer-support contractor, creating direct account-takeover, identity-fraud and voice-phishing exposure for Coinone customers and a template risk for any firm whose support desk holds customer credentials. Firms should warn staff and customers about contact purporting to come from Coinone, and review whether their own outsourced support systems hold passwords or identity documents. The exchange says its trading and wallet systems were not directly breached, so no fund losses have been reported.
breaking.headline: Coinone discloses breach via support contractor; passwords, resident registration numbers and bank account numbers may have leaked
breaking.known: Coinone, a South Korean crypto exchange, said in a notice on 15 November 2026 that an external attacker broke into the server of MetaM, the contractor that runs its customer support, at about 04:00 on 12 November, and viewed or took customer support data. Coinone learned of it from the contractor at about 09:20 the same day. The data that may have leaked is information customers gave during support chats and calls: names, email addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, bank account numbers, passwords, resident registration numbers, ID-issue dates, home addresses, wallet addresses and transaction IDs (TXIDs); which fields apply varies by customer. Coinone said its member-account, trading and wallet systems run separately from the contractor's server and it has found no sign of direct intrusion into them so far. The exact number of affected customers and the precise timing are still being established with the contractor and specialist agencies. Coinone blocked the IP addresses and access routes used, moved customer support to email-only, and reported the incident to the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA), the Personal Information Protection Commission and the Financial Supervisory Service. It warned customers about voice phishing, phishing messages and identity theft using the leaked data, and advised changing passwords and checking registered withdrawal addresses.
breaking.source_name: Coinone notice, 15 November 2026 (in Korean); Yonhap News Agency, 15 November 2026 (translated from Korean); Financial News, 15 November 2026 (translated from Korean)
breaking.summary: South Korean crypto exchange Coinone said on 15 November 2026 that an attacker broke into its customer-support contractor MetaM's server on 12 November and may have taken customer data given during support contacts, including passwords, resident registration numbers, bank account numbers and wallet addresses. The number affected is not yet confirmed; Coinone's own account, trading and wallet systems were not directly breached, it said.
breaking.type: Named BFSI victim — major data breach
breaking.unknown: The attacker and the entry route have not been disclosed, and the number of affected customers has not been confirmed. Which of the listed fields were actually taken for any given customer has not been individually established. Whether the data has been published or misused is not yet known.

breaking.bfsi_impact: A major insurer's customer portal breach exposes names, addresses, dates of birth, emails and phone numbers for about 597,000 policyholders — prime material for phishing and identity fraud impersonating AXA Direct Japan. Credit card information was not included and no misuse had been confirmed, so direct payment fraud risk is limited, but firms and customers in Japan should treat contact purporting to come from AXA as suspect and watch for follow-on impersonation, including via the roadside-assistance provider whose systems were also breached.
breaking.headline: AXA Direct Japan discloses breach; about 597,000 MyAXA accounts possibly affected
breaking.known: AXA General Insurance (AXA Direct Japan) said in a first notice on 12 November 2026 that unauthorised access to its customer portal MyAXA had been confirmed, and in a second notice on 13 November that suspicious access detected at about 08:30 on 9 November and blocked at 10:53 the same day had reached customer information it was not authorised to access. About 597,000 MyAXA accounts may have been affected; the information that may have leaked is names, addresses, dates of birth, email addresses and telephone numbers. Credit card information was not included. Part of the information leak has been confirmed; the cause and full scope remain under investigation. No misuse of the information or secondary damage had been confirmed as of the 13 November notice, and affected customers are to be contacted individually. MyAXA was suspended and resumed on 12 November after security checks. The same notices report a breach at the outsourced roadside-assistance provider, Prestige Core Solution, which detected unauthorised access to its systems on 29 October and told AXA on 2 November that some customer-related information had been taken outside its system; the range of customers and information involved there is still being examined. AXA said it stopped customer-data transfers to the provider, strengthened monitoring and reported the matter to the relevant authorities.
breaking.source_name: AXA Direct Japan notices, 12 and 13 November 2026 (in Japanese); ad-hoc-news, 13 November 2026
breaking.summary: AXA Direct Japan said on 13 November 2026 that unauthorised access to its MyAXA customer portal may have affected about 597,000 accounts, exposing names, addresses, dates of birth, email addresses and telephone numbers. Credit card information was not included; part of the leak is confirmed and no misuse had been found. Its roadside-assistance provider was also breached.
breaking.type: Named BFSI victim — major data breach
breaking.unknown: The attacker, the entry route and the exact number of accounts whose data was actually taken have not been disclosed; 597,000 is the number of accounts that may have been affected, not a confirmed count of exposed individuals. The scope of the roadside-assistance provider breach is still being examined. Whether the data has been published or misused is not yet known.

breaking.bfsi_impact: A major Japanese brokerage has exposed the email addresses of up to 1.13 million prospective account holders plus 1,592 identity-verification document images, including driving licences, My Number card fronts and selfies — prime material for phishing and identity fraud targeting Japanese investors. Account numbers and passwords were not in the affected system, so direct account-takeover risk is limited, but firms should warn staff and customers about contact purporting to come from Monex and treat the leaked addresses as active phishing targets.
breaking.headline: Monex Securities discloses breach; up to 1.13 million email addresses and 1,592 ID document images may have leaked
breaking.known: Monex Securities announced on 13 November 2026 that a third-party system used for managing online account applications was hit by unauthorised access, and that personal data held in it may have leaked. The intrusion attempt was detected by the external operator on 18 October and external access to the system was cut off on 19 October; parts of the online account-opening service remain suspended. Confirmed as possibly leaked: up to 1.13 million email addresses registered from 16 October 2019 onward as the first step of an online account application (including duplicates, incomplete entries and people who never completed opening an account), and 1,592 identity-verification document images submitted by photo-based applications, including My Number card fronts, driving licence fronts and backs, and selfies. Monex said the My Number itself (on the card reverse) was not confirmed leaked, and that account numbers, login passwords and trading passwords were stored in a separate core system and were not exposed. No fraudulent transactions or misuse of the data had been reported as of the announcement; a forensic investigation with an external specialist is continuing.
breaking.source_name: Monex Securities announcement, 13 November 2026 (in Japanese, via PR Times); TokyoReporter, 14 November 2026, reporting Jiji Press
breaking.summary: Japanese brokerage Monex Securities said on 13 November 2026 that unauthorised access to a third-party account-opening system may have exposed up to 1.13 million email addresses and 1,592 identity-verification document images, including driving licences and My Number card fronts. Account numbers and passwords were in a separate system and were not exposed; no fraudulent transactions had been reported.
breaking.type: Named BFSI victim — major data breach
breaking.unknown: The attacker, the entry route and the exact number of individuals affected have not been disclosed; the 1.13 million figure is a maximum count of email addresses, including duplicates and incomplete applications, not a confirmed count of exposed individuals. Which of the 1,592 document images were actually taken has not been individually identified. Whether the data has been published or misused is not yet known.

breaking.bfsi_impact: Brazil's largest state-owned banking group's insurance and pensions arm has lost its full customer registration base, creating large-scale identity-fraud and phishing exposure for 7.6 million people: firms with Brazilian exposure should warn customers and staff about contact purporting to come from Caixa, and treat names plus CPFs as active impersonation material. The exclusion of bank data and passwords limits direct account-takeover risk, but CPFs are the key identifier for fraud in Brazil.
breaking.headline: Caixa Vida e Previdência discloses cyberattack; registration data of 7.6 million customers copied
breaking.known: Caixa Seguridade disclosed the incident in a market notice filed with Brazil's securities regulator, the CVM, on 12 November 2026. The attack was detected on 6 November: unauthorised access to Caixa Vida e Previdência's systems and copying of personal and registration data outside its technology environment. The affected database holds the registration records of all 7.6 million active customers plus former customers; the company did not say exactly how many individuals' data was effectively exposed. Confirmed exposed so far: names and CPFs (Brazilian tax IDs), and in part of the records addresses, telephone numbers, email addresses and dates of birth. Preliminary analysis found no indication that financial or authentication data was compromised — policy values, pension balances, bank data and passwords. The company said the incident was promptly identified and contained, that a forensic investigation with a specialist consultancy is under way, and that it notified Brazil's data-protection authority, the ANPD, on 11 November. Affected customers are being contacted by email. Caixa's Pix service had unrelated instability on 12 November; no link to the attack has been established.
breaking.source_name: Olhar Digital, 12 November 2026 (translated from Portuguese); Tecnoblog, 12 November 2026 (translated from Portuguese)
breaking.summary: Caixa Vida e Previdência, the insurance and pensions arm of Brazil's state-owned Caixa group, said on 12 November 2026 that attackers copied its customer registration database, covering all 7.6 million active customers plus former customers. Names and CPFs (Brazilian tax IDs) were exposed, with addresses, phone numbers, emails and birth dates in part of the records. The company said preliminary analysis found no sign that policy values, pension balances, bank data or passwords were compromised, and no evidence the data has been published or misused.
breaking.type: Named BFSI victim — major data breach
breaking.unknown: The attacker, the entry route and the number of former customers in the copied database have not been disclosed. The 7.6 million figure is the size of the active-customer base in the affected database, not a confirmed count of exposed individuals. Whether the copied data has been or will be published or misused is not yet known.

breaking.bfsi_impact: Japanese securities firms and banks that run or rely on stockholding-association administration should check whether their own systems share the same exposure, and treat the leaked member data — names, addresses, holdings and account details — as phishing and impersonation material: affected members should be warned about contact purporting to come from SMBC Nikko or their employer about their holdings. The incident is the third disclosure in a week from SMBC Group companies, so firms should also review whether group-wide or shared-service weaknesses are in play. There is no trading impact: the affected system cannot execute share trades.
breaking.headline: SMBC Nikko Securities discloses breach of employee stockholding-association system; up to 56,487 members' data may have leaked
breaking.known: SMBC Nikko Securities announced on 11 November 2026 that its system for administering employee stockholding associations (mochikabu-kai) — used to run the share-purchase schemes of listed companies — suffered unauthorised access by a third party, and personal data of up to 56,487 members may have leaked. The firm detected an anomaly on 7 November, confirmed the unauthorised access on 9 November, blocked access and temporarily suspended the service the same day; its investigation then confirmed the leak. The data leaked or possibly leaked includes stockholding-association names, investment holdings, member identification numbers, names, addresses, dividends and taxes, shareholding balances and transfer-destination account information — though the fields vary by association and not every member had every field exposed. Telephone numbers and email addresses were not registered in the system and did not leak. The system cannot execute share trades, so no unauthorised trading is possible through it. The company said no secondary harm had been confirmed at the time of disclosure, that it would contact affected associations individually, and warned members to beware of suspicious contact. The disclosure was published by NHK at 15:34 JST (14:34 SGT) on 11 November — in the 12:00-16:00 window — but was missed by the 16:00 wire check and picked up by this check; it is a separate incident from the SMBC Consumer Finance breach of 5 November and the SMBC email-contractor leak, involving a different SMBC Group company and system.
breaking.source_name: NHK, 11 November 2026 (translated from Japanese); TV Asahi (ANN), 11 November 2026 (translated from Japanese); Kyodo News, 11 November 2026 (translated from Japanese)
breaking.summary: SMBC Nikko Securities said on 11 November 2026 that unauthorised access to the system it uses to administer employee stockholding associations may have leaked personal data of up to 56,487 members. The firm detected an anomaly on 7 November, confirmed the access on 9 November and stopped the service the same day. Leaked or possibly leaked data includes names, addresses, holdings, dividends and transfer-destination account details; phone numbers and email addresses were not held in the system. No secondary harm had been confirmed at disclosure, and the system cannot execute share trades. This is a separate incident from the SMBC Consumer Finance breach (5 November) and the SMBC email-contractor leak — a different SMBC Group company and system.
breaking.type: Named BFSI victim — major data breach
breaking.unknown: The attacker and the entry route have not been disclosed; the investigation is ongoing. The 56,487 figure is a maximum — the fields leaked vary by stockholding association, and not every member had every field exposed. Whether any of the leaked data has been misused beyond the confirmed leak is not yet known.

breaking.bfsi_impact: Korean banks, insurers and securities firms should treat the leak as a targeting and impersonation risk: the exposed material is administrative forms and staff contact details from the evaluation process — the FSI says no vulnerability-assessment results, system diagrams or customer sensitive credit information were in the system — which could still be used to pick follow-on targets or to craft convincing impersonation of the FSI or regulators. Firms should check what they submitted through the evaluation system, watch for phishing citing the FSI or the evaluation process, and review whether staff contact details in the leaked documents need resetting. The breach of the sector's own security overseer — in the middle of a wave of 40 incidents at 37 firms — also raises the stakes for the FSC's sector-wide inspections.
breaking.headline: South Korea's Financial Security Institute hacked; financial firms' security-assessment data leaked
breaking.known: The Financial Security Institute (FSI), the Financial Services Commission-affiliated body that oversees cybersecurity for South Korea's financial sector, detected on 9 November that its 'information-security continuous evaluation' site had been hacked and reported it to the Financial Services Commission and other authorities; access was blocked. The system supports security-state evaluations of financial firms — about 3,000 firms were in scope for this year's evaluation, per an FSI press release in April — and the leaked material is assessment-support documents submitted by firms, with some personal information contained in those documents also exposed, including email addresses according to the Seoul Economic Daily. The FSI has notified individual financial firms of the leak. The site now shows a notice saying the server is temporarily suspended for service reorganisation. Financial authorities said the breach of the body that monitors financial-sector security must be treated seriously for trust reasons and have demanded a thorough check and measures to prevent recurrence. No hack of the Financial Services Commission or the Financial Supervisory Service has been reported. On 10 November the FSI quantified the leak (reported by Digital Daily, 10 November 22:58, and Seoul Shinmun, 11 November print edition): about 200 administrative forms, about 300 personal-information items (names and dates of birth contained in the forms) and about 350 masked system-user records; Seoul Shinmun reported material from 30-40 of the roughly 3,000 firms in scope leaked. The FSI said the system collects administrative forms only and holds no vulnerability-analysis evaluation results, system diagrams, resident registration numbers or customer sensitive credit information, and that it reported the incident to the Financial Services Commission and the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA). On 11 November the FSI confirmed the affected firms number 48, all of them mutual-finance institutions — local agricultural cooperatives, credit unions and forestry cooperatives — with no large firm and no institution from another financial sector affected; this supersedes the earlier press estimate of 30-40 firms. The leaked files number about 130. The attack used a fake account with Financial Supervisory Service-level privileges created by exploiting a flaw in the FSI's authorisation process; no actual FSS account or account information was compromised. All 246 IP addresses used in the attack were domestic Korean addresses (revised up from 236 on 13 November), none overlapping with IPs from previously known hacking attempts, and the attacker rotated through hundreds of IPs, with the attack concentrated on the afternoon of 9 November (about 13:00-14:00) before the FSI blocked access at 14:19. The Financial Services Commission began an on-site inspection at the FSI on the morning of 11 November, with FSS staff assisting, and the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency's cyber investigation unit has opened an investigation after the FSI asked police to trace the attack IPs. The FSI has cancelled the VIP event for its FISCON 2026 financial information-security conference, which had been scheduled for 12 November. On 12 November the Dong-A Ilbo reported that about 850 records containing personal information had been exposed — a higher count than the FSI's earlier estimate of about 300 personal-information items, and the two figures have not been reconciled — and that the assessment system had already been flagged in a 2022 Financial Services Commission special audit as vulnerable to data leaks; the FSI apologised for the breach. The Financial Services Commission's on-site inspection at the FSI, begun on the morning of 11 November, continued on 12 November. (Dong-A Ilbo, 12 November 2026; Herald Business, 12 November 2026) On 12 November FSI president Park Sang-won publicly apologised in person at the opening of the FISCON 2026 financial information-security conference in Seoul, pledged a full inspection of all FSI systems and fundamental measures to prevent recurrence, and said the institute was still determining whether additional data had leaked; the conference went ahead as scheduled with its VIP events cancelled. (NoCut News, 12 November 2026; SBS, 12 November 2026) On 12 November the Financial Services Commission said it would open a special audit of the FSI from 16 November, with experts and related agencies taking part. (Newsis, 12 November 2026, translated from Korean; etoday, 12 November 2026, translated from Korean) On 13 November the Financial Services Commission released a detailed timeline to the National Assembly (reported by Yonhap via Maeil Business Newspaper, 13 November 2026, translated from Korean): the FSI detected abnormal access at 10:50 on 9 November, confirmed a webshell attack at 13:54 that failed because of file-encryption policy, detected an unauthorised login attempt at 14:11, stopped the service at 14:19 and confirmed the data leak at 15:50; the initial investigation ran 15:58-23:05 that day, an emergency committee met at 13:30 on 10 November, the FSC was notified at 14:41 and a formal incident report filed at 15:48, the Personal Information Protection Commission was notified at 21:45 on 11 November, and all 246 attack IP addresses were blocked on 12 November. The attack used an SMS-authentication bypass vulnerability in normal member registration to create a fake account, then exploited insufficient access-permission verification in the evaluation system's operator check function to download files. All 246 IPs were domestic Korean addresses; the authorities cautioned that some IPs cannot be attributed to a country and that a Korean IP does not rule out routing through proxies. The Financial Supervisory Service issued a consumer warning on 12 November about voice phishing impersonating community centres and financial institutions. (Maeil Business Newspaper, 13 November 2026, translated from Korean; Woman Economy, 13 November 2026, translated from Korean)
breaking.source_name: Yonhap, 10 November 2026 (translated from Korean); Seoul Economic Daily (English), 10 November 2026; Digital Daily and Seoul Shinmun, 11 November 2026 (translated from Korean); Yonhap, 11 November 2026 (translated from Korean); Herald Business (English), 11 November 2026; Dong-A Ilbo, 12 November 2026; Herald Business, 12 November 2026; NoCut News, 12 November 2026; SBS, 12 November 2026; Newsis, 12 November 2026 (translated from Korean); etoday, 12 November 2026 (translated from Korean); Maeil Business Newspaper, 13 November 2026 (translated from Korean); Woman Economy, 13 November 2026 (translated from Korean)
breaking.summary: South Korea's Financial Security Institute (FSI), the Financial Services Commission-affiliated body that oversees cybersecurity for the country's financial sector, said on 10 November 2026 that its information-security continuous-evaluation site was hacked. The system supports security-state evaluations of financial firms, and assessment-support documents submitted by firms leaked, with some personal information in those documents possibly exposed. The institute detected the intrusion on 9 November, blocked access and reported it to the Financial Services Commission and other authorities. The incident comes amid a wave of breaches across Korean financial firms — the FSC said on 5 November that 40 incidents had been reported at 37 firms.
breaking.type: Named BFSI victim — sector security body breached
breaking.unknown: The attacker's identity is still unknown, and whether the FSI itself was specifically targeted — rather than hit opportunistically — is still an open question raised by Korean press. The leak scope (about 130 files, about 200 administrative forms, about 300 personal-information items and about 350 masked system-user records) is still described as estimated, not final. The FSI's 10 November statement quantified about 300 personal-information items leaked, superseding the earlier line reported by Yonhap that no personal information had leaked; the Seoul Economic Daily and MoneyToday had reported personal data, including email addresses, exposed.

breaking.bfsi_impact: Peer brokerages and banks in South Korea should treat the wave of attacks on financial firms as ongoing: the same pattern — abnormal external access to web-facing login and internal systems — has now hit a major brokerage days after the regulator disclosed 40 incidents at 37 firms. Firms should review web login and groupware access controls, watch for phishing and impersonation using the exposed employee contact details and customer account numbers, and check whether staff credentials need resetting given the encrypted passwords exposed.
breaking.headline: Mirae Asset Securities discloses breach of 3,800 customer account numbers and 35,255 employee records
breaking.known: The firm said abnormal external access was detected on 4 November against its mobile-web phone-authentication login service and on 5 November against its internal groupware system (mi-global); the access routes were blocked immediately and an emergency response was activated. About 3,800 customers' account numbers were exposed; the firm says no account-holder names or other sensitive customer information leaked with them. Personal data of 35,255 current employees, retirees and outsourced staff was also exposed, including names, employee numbers, email addresses, mobile phone numbers and encrypted passwords. Resident registration numbers, passport numbers, driver's licence numbers and other unique identifiers were not exposed. The firm's co-CEOs apologised in a public notice. The incident was reported to the Financial Services Commission, the Financial Supervisory Service and the Personal Information Protection Commission. The disclosure follows a wave of breaches across South Korean financial firms — the FSC said on 5 November that 40 incidents had been reported at 37 firms — and is a separate incident from the 28 October Mirae Asset Global Investments disclosure, which involved a different entity and no customer data. Newspim reported on 7 November that this is the fourth intrusion in the Mirae Asset Group in recent weeks, after customer data leaked from Mirae Asset Life on 26 October and intrusion attempts at Mirae Asset Asset Management on 28 October and Energy Infrastructure Asset Management on 2 November; the firm has not said the incidents are linked. Separately, on 12 November South Korea's Ministry of Economy and Finance said it had begun a full review of the hacking of the Government Fund Investment Pool website run by Mirae Asset Global Investments — the 28 October incident — after undisclosed data including fund returns on tens of trillions of won in state funds was taken and personal data of about 331 users, mostly public officials and public-institution staff, leaked; the ministry's Fund Asset Management Policy Committee will meet on 13 November to establish the details. (NoCut News, 12 November 2026, translated from Korean)
breaking.source_name: AlphaBiz, 7 November 2026 (translated from Korean); Korea Times, 7 November 2026; NoCut News, 12 November 2026 (translated from Korean)
breaking.summary: Mirae Asset Securities, one of South Korea's largest brokerages, said on 7 November 2026 that external attacks on 4–5 November exposed the account numbers of about 3,800 customers and personal data of 35,255 current and former employees and contractors, including names, employee numbers, email addresses, mobile phone numbers and encrypted passwords. The firm says no malware infection or service disruption occurred, no financial loss has been confirmed, and its main systems are operating normally. The incident was reported to the Financial Services Commission, the Financial Supervisory Service and the Personal Information Protection Commission.
breaking.type: Named BFSI victim — major data breach
breaking.unknown: The attack method and the attacker's identity are undisclosed, and the firm has not said how the attackers reached the two systems. Whether the exposed account numbers or employee data have been misused has not been reported.

breaking.bfsi_impact: Malaysian banks and APAC peers should watch for a formal statement from Bank Rakyat and for any leaked data sample, and warn customers against phishing that cites the incident. The claim of internal access, if true, would make this a breach rather than a defacement; until the bank confirms or denies it, treat the internal-access claim as unconfirmed and the website defacement and outage as confirmed.
breaking.headline: Bank Rakyat website defaced by actor claiming internal access; bank confirms outage
breaking.known: Pages on the bank's official web portal, including informational pages on personal financing, were briefly defaced on the evening of 6 November; the defacement was first reported on social media and the pages were restored within about an hour. The defacement notice read: “Marlanwg is here. We have successfully accessed the internal infrastructure and retrieved a sample of your data to verify the extent of the breach”, and directed bank officials to the encrypted messaging app Session to negotiate data deletion and remediation terms. At 23:45 on 6 November the bank said its corporate website was unavailable and told customers to use its iRakyat, BRICK, QR2E and i-bizRAKYAT apps and platforms. Bank Negara Malaysia previously fined Bank Rakyat RM1 million under its Risk Management in Technology framework after a separate cybersecurity breach. On 7 November the bank said in a Facebook statement, reported by Malay Mail, that the disruption was caused by a technical problem involving a third-party service provider, that only its corporate website was affected, and that deposits, personal information and banking services were unaffected, with restoration work under way. Communications Minister Fahmi Fadzil said the same day that the incident was confined to changes to the website's appearance on a third-party-managed site, that the bank had reported the site had been hacked but the incident was limited to web defacement and takeover, and that no data theft had been detected so far; the affected server was blocked and users redirected to the i-Rakyat website, which the bank fully owns.
breaking.source_name: Pokde.Net, 6 November 2026; Siakap Keli, 6 November 2026 (translated from Malay); Malay Mail, 7 November 2026
breaking.summary: Malaysian cooperative bank Bank Rakyat's corporate website was briefly defaced on the evening of 6 November 2026 by an actor using the handle “Marlanwg”, who claimed to have accessed the bank's internal infrastructure and taken a sample of its data. The bank confirmed at 23:45 that its corporate website was unavailable and directed customers to its mobile apps and digital platforms. On 7 November the bank attributed the disruption to a technical problem involving a third-party service provider and said deposits, personal information and banking services were unaffected; the Communications Minister said the incident was limited to web defacement of a third-party-managed site with no data theft detected. The actor's claim of internal access and data theft remains unconfirmed and is now disputed by the bank.
breaking.unknown: The bank has not issued a formal statement specifically addressing the actor's claim of internal network access or data theft; it attributes the outage to a third-party technical fault and says no data was stolen. A local threat-intelligence account claims to have verified samples shared by the actor and says the data appears authentic, but this has not been independently confirmed and conflicts with the bank's and the minister's statements. Whether customer data or funds are affected, and whether the bank's wider digital services are fully restored, is unconfirmed.

breaking.bfsi_impact: Peer banks and consumer-finance firms that outsource loan guarantees should check whether their customers' data passed through the affected system, prepare for phishing and identity-fraud attempts using the leaked licence numbers and income data, and warn affected customers not to trust calls, emails or messages that cite their loan details. The leak of driver's licence numbers together with income and guarantee amounts is directly usable for impersonation and social engineering against bank customers.
breaking.headline: SMBC Consumer Finance discloses breach of up to 320,118 customers' data
breaking.known: SMBC Consumer Finance detected unauthorised access to its loan-guarantee system on 2 November and cut off access the same day; data was sent outside the company. The leaked data includes names, addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, email addresses, driver's licence numbers, employer and income details, and guarantee amounts and other contract information. Images of identity documents were not included. The firm provides guarantee services to 189 financial institutions, including regional banks, credit unions and online banks; its own Promise consumer-finance service does not use the affected system and is unaffected. No secondary harm from misuse of the data had been confirmed at the time of disclosure. Since the disclosure, partner banks have confirmed their customers are among those affected: Docomo SMTB Net Bank said up to 122,635 of its customers may be affected; Hiroshima Bank said personal data of customers who applied for two of its loan products was in the leak and suspended web applications for them; Chugoku Bank said up to 25 records were affected and also suspended web applications. (Nikkei, 6 November 2026.) Ehime Bank also said its customers' data was among the leaked records and that it was still checking how many were affected (thecoauthor, 8 November 2026). The Resona group said on 6 November that 5,935 former customers across its three banks — Resona Bank (139), Kansai Mirai Bank (5,793) and Minato Bank (3) — were affected, all with card loans already closed; Bank of Yokohama also confirmed its customers were affected, without giving a number. (Pasqualepillitteri.it, 8 November 2026, citing the Resona group disclosure and Kanagawa Shimbun.) On 10 November, Fukuoka Financial Group said at an interim-results press conference that customer information of its three banks — Kumamoto Bank, Fukuoka Bank and Juhachi-Shinwa Bank — had leaked via the SMBC Consumer Finance guarantee system; the banks apologised, and the number of affected customers is still being checked. (Kumamoto Nichinichi Shimbun, 10 November 2026, translated from Japanese.)
breaking.source_name: Nikkei, 5 November 2026; TBS NEWS DIG, 5 November 2026 (translated from Japanese); Resona group disclosure via Pasqualepillitteri.it, 8 November 2026
breaking.summary: SMBC Consumer Finance, the Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group consumer-finance arm, said on 5 November 2026 that unauthorised access to its loan-guarantee system exposed personal data of up to 320,118 people, including names, birth dates, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, driver's licence numbers, employer details, income and loan guarantee amounts. The intrusion was detected on 2 November and access was cut off the same day; the guarantee system is suspended while checks continue. No misuse of the data has been confirmed so far, and images of identity documents were not included. The data covers customers of 189 partner banks, credit unions and online banks for which the firm provides loan guarantees; its own Promise consumer-finance service was not affected.
breaking.type: Named BFSI victim — major data breach
breaking.unknown: The full list of affected partner institutions is still being pinned down — Hiroshima Bank, Chugoku Bank, Docomo SMTB Net Bank, Ehime Bank and the three Fukuoka Financial Group banks have confirmed their customers are affected. Whether the intrusion exploited a specific vulnerability, and the attacker's identity, are undisclosed.

breaking.bfsi_impact: A leaked list of 227,216 corporate customer email addresses is ready-made fuel for targeted phishing and business-email compromise impersonating SMBC. Peer banks using third-party email-delivery services should check their own suppliers' exposure, and customers should treat any message citing SMBC business as suspect unless verified through known channels.
breaking.headline: Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation confirms 227,216 email addresses leaked via contractor
breaking.known: The leak came through Arara's email-delivery service 'Arara Message', used by the bank. The affected addresses are recipients of bank emails sent 1 July–31 October 2026, mainly corporate customers plus some sole proprietors. No account numbers, balances, PINs or internet-banking IDs or passwords were included. The bank was told of the unauthorised access on 28 October and received confirmation that data had leaked on 2 November. SMBC and SMBC Trust Bank also announced a new information-sharing arrangement with Japan's National Police Agency from 9 November to speed up anti-fraud cooperation.
breaking.source_name: TBS NEWS DIG, 5 November 2026 (translated from Japanese)
breaking.summary: Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation said on 5 November 2026 that unauthorised access to its email-delivery contractor Arara's 'Arara Message' service leaked 227,216 email addresses — the recipients of emails the bank sent between 1 July and 31 October, mainly corporate customers and some sole proprietors. No account numbers, balances, PINs or internet-banking IDs or passwords were included. The bank was told of the unauthorised access on 28 October and received confirmation of the leak on 2 November.
breaking.type: Named BFSI victim — third-party data breach
breaking.unknown: The cause of the unauthorised access at the contractor and the full extent of any further exposure are still being checked with the contractor. Whether any leaked addresses have been used in phishing has not been reported.

breaking.bfsi_impact: Peer banks using third-party or supplier-built mobile banking systems should review supplier security settings, account-enumeration controls and verification for non-designated transfers, and check whether any supplier system permits transfers without the customer logging in. breaking.headline: Bank SinoPac confirms hackers exploited supplier flaw in unauthorised transfers
breaking.known: At a press conference on the evening of 4 November, reported by Focus Taiwan (CNA) at 21:01 SGT, the bank said external hackers breached security settings at the supplier of its new online banking transaction system, used trial-and-error to obtain valid accounts sharing an ID-number prefix, and moved funds to a single Taipei Fubon Bank account, which was frozen. The bank said it reimbursed customers on 3 November, found no evidence of personal-data leakage, hired an independent cybersecurity team, shared threat information with peers via F-ISAC, and will seek compensation from the foreign supplier, whose system is used by no other bank in Taiwan. Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission requires a detailed major-incident report by 12 November. On 12 November Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission said at its regular press conference that the bank's detailed investigation report was due that day and had not yet been received, though the regulator expected it the same day; the FSC said it would review whether the bank carried out proper due diligence on its outsourced vendors and did not rule out fines, and it convened bank chief information security officers the same day to discuss the shift in attack patterns brought by artificial intelligence. (BigGo Finance, 12 November 2026, translated from Chinese; Mirror Daily, 12 November 2026, translated from Chinese)
breaking.source_name: Focus Taiwan (CNA), 4 November 2026; BigGo Finance, 12 November 2026 (translated from Chinese); Mirror Daily, 12 November 2026 (translated from Chinese)
breaking.summary: Taiwan's Bank SinoPac said on 4 November 2026 that external hackers exploited security settings at the supplier of its new mobile banking system, causing 427 unauthorised transfers totalling about NT$41.76 million (about US$1.27 million) on 3 November. The bank has reimbursed affected customers, the single receiving account at another bank was frozen, and the new system has been suspended.
breaking.unknown: The supplier's name, the exact flaw in its security settings, and the attackers' identity are undisclosed, and the case is under criminal investigation. Local reports of the bank's press conference put the affected customer count at 418, against the Financial Supervisory Commission / Focus Taiwan figure of 419 accounts for the same 427 transfers; the wire uses the regulator's figure and flags the one-customer discrepancy.

breaking.bfsi_impact: A named European bank victim with fraudulent transactions: peer banks should review controls on large and exchange-account withdrawals, verify transaction authorisation and suspension procedures, and watch for laundering of any linked funds through exchanges and instant-swap services. Under the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act, major ICT incidents carry a short initial reporting window, so EU-regulated peers should check their own incident-classification clocks. Third-party platform access is now a confirmed route in this case: review service-provider platforms that can reach the bank directly, not only customer-facing channels.
breaking.headline: Crédit Mutuel Arkéa confirms cyberattack enabling fraudulent transactions
breaking.known: The bank's own statement, reported by CoinDesk, Bloomberg and Ledger Insights on 4 November, confirms the attack and the fraudulent transactions. Blockchain investigator ZachXBT first flagged a suspected loss of more than $106 million at an unnamed EU entity on 2 November and named Arkéa on 3 November, putting the total above $133 million; Bitquery traced $108.8 million in USDC withdrawals from Kraken, Crypto.com and OKX accounts over 1–2 November, and Crypto.com said it blocked funds linked to the incident. In a further statement on the evening of 4 November, reported by AFP/Reuters and updated by CNA at 00:57 SGT on 5 November, the bank said attackers reached Arkéa directly through the platform of one of its service providers — not through Fortuneo, and not through client accounts — used the bank's own account to transfer funds to other banks, and then converted funds into cryptocurrency via specialist platforms; a portion of funds was blocked and recovery efforts are under way. The bank gave a provisional estimate of about €100 million, validated the order of magnitude of the reported $133 million (about €118 million) figure, but has not confirmed a final figure. The Paris public prosecutor's office has opened an investigation into an attack on an automated data processing system by an organised group. On 5 November the bank said nearly all operations had resumed after security checks and additional safeguards, customer funds were unaffected, and the losses were lower than the $133 million figure reported in the press and not of a nature to undermine the group's financial strength. On 6 November the president of the Crédit Mutuel confederation, Daniel Baal, told France 5 television that the bank had “already recovered part of (the missing money) today”, without saying how much; Le Télégramme put the amount taken at €118 million.
breaking.source_name: Reuters / AFP via CNA, 4-5 November 2026; Cointelegraph, 5 November 2026
breaking.summary: French banking group Crédit Mutuel Arkéa confirmed on 4 November 2026 that it was the target of a cyberattack that enabled fraudulent transactions. The bank says the incident is now under control, some transactions were temporarily suspended, regulators and supervisory authorities have been notified, and clients face no financial consequences. In its evening update the bank gave a provisional estimate of about €100 million, with the final figure still being assessed.
breaking.unknown: The bank has not confirmed a final amount, the attack method, which service provider's platform was used, whether the provider itself was breached (reported by Le Figaro, not confirmed by the bank), or how much, if anything, has been recovered. The $133 million figure is the investigator's estimate, repeated in the press, not a bank-confirmed loss; the bank has validated only its order of magnitude.

entries.bfsi_impact: Infoblox DNS, DHCP and identity products are widely deployed in BFSI networks, so customer NIOS configuration data in attacker hands could support targeted follow-on attacks against customer environments; firms using Infoblox should watch for a direct notification and review any third-party access to their own collaboration systems. Employee Social Security numbers and direct-deposit details also raise phishing and identity-fraud risk for Infoblox staff. entries.headline: Infoblox confirms breach via third-party SharePoint migration vendor; customer NIOS data and employee records exposed
entries.known: Networking and security firm Infoblox confirmed on 16 November 2026 that attackers accessed company information through a compromised third-party data-migration vendor, using the vendor's trusted access to exfiltrate data from Infoblox's Microsoft SharePoint. The Register reported on 16 November 2026 that the data included configuration information for some customers' NIOS (Network Identity Operating System) deployments, covering DNS, DHCP, Grid databases and reporting logs, and that employee data was also taken, including direct-deposit details, contact information, dates of birth and Social Security numbers for employees and dependents. Infoblox said it activated incident response, hired outside cybersecurity experts, terminated work with the vendor, and sent notifications to affected parties. It says it has no indication that any Infoblox products, cloud services, software updates or build-and-release processes were involved.
entries.source_name: The Register, 16 November 2026; TechCrunch, 16 November 2026
entries.summary: Infoblox confirmed on 16 November 2026 that attackers used a compromised third-party data-migration vendor's trusted access to take company data from its Microsoft SharePoint, including customer NIOS deployment configuration and employee records with Social Security numbers and direct-deposit details. Infoblox says its products, cloud services and build processes were not involved; the number affected is not disclosed.
entries.type: Confirmed vendor breach — networking and security vendor
entries.unknown: How many customers and employees are affected, the identity of the compromised vendor, who the attacker is, and whether any of the data has been published or misused.

entries.bfsi_impact: Barracuda Managed XDR and Monitored Endpoint customers that the firm contacted directly should reissue integration credentials and review connected-system activity from 1 November 2026; other customers need take no action, Barracuda says. For BFSI firms the case is a template warning on unretired vendor keys and on AI-tool-driven intrusion speed, and the confirmed ARTEX link is directly relevant to the offensive-AI-tooling tracker.
entries.headline: Barracuda confirms cloud breach via unretired vendor key and ARTEX AI framework; about 10 cloud accounts accessed
entries.known: Barracuda Networks disclosed that an attacker used a cloud access key it had issued to a third-party AI company for an earlier project and never retired. The key was stored in a configuration file in the vendor's GitHub repository and was apparently stolen when the vendor's development environment was compromised in October. The attacker entered about 10 of Barracuda's cloud accounts over a 44-hour period on 1-2 November 2026, moving through a data-analytics environment, source-code repositories and Kubernetes clusters, and a second attempt to create a new cloud administrator identity was blocked. The intrusion was discovered on 4 November, when an engineer noticed odd activity on their own account. Barracuda says the attack used machine-style labels, probing methods and hunting routines matching ARTEX, the open-source AI pentesting framework, and that it was financially motivated. Barracuda published a Trust Center advisory on 10 November 2026, updated 13 November, and its CISO posted on 11 November; BleepingComputer reported the incident on 16 November 2026. Barracuda says it found no direct evidence that XDR customer integration credentials were viewed, but has told some customers to reissue them as a precaution.
entries.source_name: BleepingComputer, 16 November 2026; Barracuda Trust Center advisory, 10 November 2026 (updated 13 November)
entries.summary: Barracuda Networks disclosed that an attacker used a cloud access key issued to a third-party AI vendor and never retired — apparently taken from a config file in the vendor's GitHub repository — to enter about 10 of its cloud accounts over 44 hours on 1-2 November 2026, using the open-source ARTEX AI pentesting framework. The intrusion was found on 4 November. Barracuda says it found no direct evidence XDR customer integration credentials were viewed, but has told some customers to reissue them as a precaution.
entries.type: Confirmed vendor breach — security vendor, AI tooling
entries.unknown: Which cloud the key belonged to, whether the vendor's GitHub repository was public or private, whether any XDR customer integration credentials were actually viewed — Barracuda says its logging was not detailed enough to rule it out — and who the attacker is.

The published claims include 65,000 payment-card photographs, personal photographs, identity-document photographs, 8,000 financial records reportedly containing passwords, and 11,000 customer records. entries.type: Alleged data leak — Brazilian credit lender, unverified

Nothing is confirmed, so the impact is watch-level; issuers should watch for phishing citing Banco Carrefour and for the separately mentioned transaction-history dataset appearing for sale.

entries.bfsi_impact: A payment fintech holding IBANs, card tokens and KYC data is a direct fraud enabler if that data was taken: IBANs plus identity documents support impersonation and invoice fraud, and password hashes invite credential-stuffing where passwords are reused. The confirmed facts so far are service suspension and indications of theft, not a confirmed exfiltration volume, so the impact is watch-level; firms should warn staff and customers about phishing citing CrediBill and check for reuse of CrediBill credentials.
entries.headline: Swiss fintech CrediBill suspends service after cyberattack; new findings point to data theft
entries.known: Swiss bill-payment fintech CrediBill (a Bottomline-owned service for paying invoices by card) has taken its systems offline after a cyberattack that began on 11 November 2026; customers cannot log in or use the service. CEO Alexander Segmuller said the firm acted quickly to protect customer data and that in-house staff and a Swiss security firm are investigating. Up to midday on 14 November the investigation had found no proof that data had left the business; the latest findings now point to data having been taken without permission, though Segmuller said it is not yet clear which data is affected. Two categories of data may be at risk: personal data such as contact details, ID and KYC data and password hashes, and transaction data including IBANs, card tokens and bills. The firm says it has never held card numbers and stores cards only as tokens. CrediBill has reported the case to the Swiss data protection office, filed a criminal complaint, and a police cybercrime unit is involved. Once the service returns, each user must set a new password on first login; users who reuse their CrediBill password elsewhere should change it there at once. Reported 16 November 2026 by Fintech News Switzerland, quoting the CEO.
entries.source_name: Fintech News Switzerland, 16 November 2026 (reporting CrediBill's statements and CEO Alexander Segmuller)
entries.summary: Swiss bill-payment fintech CrediBill said on 16 November that its service has been suspended since an attack that began on 11 November, and that new findings point to data having been taken; personal data including ID and KYC details and password hashes, and transaction data including IBANs and card tokens, may be affected. The scope is still unclear.
entries.type: Named BFSI victim — fintech breach, possible data theft
entries.unknown: Which data, if any, was actually exfiltrated and how many customers are affected; the attack method and whether a ransom was demanded; when the service will reopen.

entries.bfsi_impact: A template risk for any lender whose disbursement flow trusts whitelisted cloud IP addresses: fraudsters register on the same public clouds, send payout commands that look routine, and sit undetected for a week because reconciliation runs weekly or fortnightly. The use of an AI platform (CyberStrikeAI) to generate command scripts at bulk speed, and a nationwide total above Rs 300 crore across 150+ NBFC complaints, marks Indian NBFCs as a sustained target class; firms should reconcile disbursements daily, review cloud IP whitelists, and audit front-end and payout APIs.
entries.headline: Delhi Police: 12 NBFCs in Delhi-NCR lost over Rs 65 crore to cyber fraud in three months; AI tools used in the attacks
entries.known: Delhi Police told The Indian Express on 16 November 2026 that 12 non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) in Delhi-NCR lost over Rs 65 crore (about US$7.3 million) to cyber fraud in the past three months. The FIRs are part of more than 150 complaints filed by NBFCs across India in the same period, totalling more than Rs 300 crore stolen. Police say attackers use malware to breach the front end of an NBFC's app, dwell for seven to eight days identifying loans approved but not yet disbursed, then send payout commands from cloud-server IP addresses the NBFC's firewall already whitelists, replacing the borrower's account number with a mule account. Rs 18 crore of the Rs 65 crore was detected and seized before it left mule accounts; 20 people have been arrested in the 12 NCR cases. Named cases: Hero FinCorp lost Rs 12 crore on 17 August 2026 through 317 transactions using at least 165 IP addresses; Unifinz Pvt Ltd lost Rs 12.49 crore on 21 October through 550 transactions over two days. In one October case an NBFC was duped of Rs 3 crore and the investigation found the Chinese AI platform CyberStrikeAI was used to send command scripts to the NBFC. Delhi Police and CERT-In have issued advisories to NBFCs. This is a distinct pattern from the Telangana 'Crafty Falcon' payout-API wave already on the wire (entry-nbfc-payout-api-20261114): different region, and loan-diversion rather than payout-API exploitation.
entries.source_name: The Indian Express, 16 November 2026
entries.summary: Delhi Police say 12 NBFCs in Delhi-NCR lost over Rs 65 crore in three months to hackers diverting approved-but-undisbursed loans to mule accounts; nationwide, more than 150 NBFC complaints total over Rs 300 crore, and police say the AI platform CyberStrikeAI was used in one October case.
entries.type: Loan-disbursement fraud wave — Indian NBFCs
entries.unknown: The names of 10 of the 12 Delhi-NCR NBFCs; whether the Delhi-NCR cases share infrastructure with the Telangana 'Crafty Falcon' payout-API wave; how many of the 150+ nationwide complaints are confirmed fraud versus attempts.

entries.bfsi_impact: A confirmed exchange breach with a novel control failure — a custodian's freeze could not stop transfers signed with the exchange's own backup keys — is a template risk for any firm relying on multisignature custody; customer PII exposure also feeds phishing and identity fraud against Unocoin customers. The loss is small (under 1% of customer holdings) and Unocoin is covering it, so the direct market impact is limited, but the backup-key handling failure is the lesson for custody arrangements.
entries.headline: Indian exchange Unocoin confirms about $200,000 taken from three hot wallets; customer data may have been exposed
entries.known: Indian crypto exchange Unocoin said on 14 November 2026 that attackers took about $200,000 in cryptocurrency from three of its more than 20 operational hot wallets, signing the transfers with encrypted paper backup keys generated about eight years ago; the keys were compromised and a decryption passphrase existed within the compromised infrastructure. BitGo's investigation, published 13 November, found the transfers were signed with Unocoin-controlled user and backup keys and broadcast directly to the blockchain, bypassing the BitGo account freeze; BitGo says its systems were not compromised and its key was never used. Unocoin detected suspicious activity on 6 November, suspended all services on 9 November, and they remain suspended with no restoration date. Unocoin will cover the loss from its own funds and customer balances will not be reduced. Customer emails, home addresses, encrypted passwords, KYC details and balances may have been exposed; Unocoin says it has not found evidence that customer KYC documents were accessed. Bitquery's figures (98 transfers, $182,270, 9-11 November; plus about 39,167 XRP, about $42,700, from another wallet) do not reconcile exactly with Unocoin's about $200,000 estimate. Flagged for the wire by the 15 November evening deep-research check.
entries.source_name: Unocoin security incident update, 14 November 2026; BitGo, 13 November 2026
entries.summary: Indian crypto exchange Unocoin confirmed on 14 November that attackers used its compromised paper backup keys to take about $200,000 from three hot wallets; customer emails, addresses, encrypted passwords and KYC details may have been exposed, and all services remain suspended since 9 November.
entries.type: Exchange breach — backup-key compromise
entries.unknown: How the attackers obtained the encrypted backup keys and the decryption passphrase; the exact total loss (Unocoin's about $200,000 estimate versus Bitquery's figures); when services will reopen; whether any customer data was actually accessed.

entries.bfsi_impact: La Poste group owns La Banque Postale, and Maileva handles financial documents — payslips, invoices, shareholder meeting notices — for more than 70,000 business clients, so the exposed names and postal addresses of 22 million recipients support phishing, social-engineering and identity-fraud targeting, including of bank customers. The billing data also holds business clients' IBANs, which can feed president/CEO fraud; direct account-takeover risk for recipients is low because their bank details were not compromised. Firms whose mail Maileva handles should expect customer queries and watch for phishing using the exposed details.
entries.headline: La Poste subsidiary Maileva confirms breach exposing names and addresses of 22 million people; business clients' IBANs also in billing data
entries.known: A mid-September cyberattack on Maileva, a Docaposte business in the La Poste group that prints and posts documents such as payslips, registered letters, invoices and shareholder meeting notices for more than 70,000 business clients, stole the first names, surnames and postal addresses of 22 million recipients, La Poste confirmed to AFP on 14 November 2026. About 39 million mail references were in the compromised database, equal to 22 million distinct people after deduplication. Maileva suspended services on 23 September and resumed on 29 September. Maileva says bank details were not affected; it has notified France's CNIL, filed a criminal complaint, and a judicial investigation is under way. This item was confirmed before the 20:00 wire check on 15 November and missed by it. On 15 November 2026 the Paris prosecutor's office confirmed it had opened a criminal investigation, assigned to the BL2C cybercrime brigade. Docaposte's 5 October information sheet also describes a second data set, from the OpenCell billing application, covering business clients' billing contacts, invoice amounts and IBANs; Maileva's statement that bank details were not affected refers to the 22 million recipients, while the IBANs belong to business clients.
entries.source_name: Security Affairs, 15 November 2026; Le Temps / AFP, 14 November 2026; MACCUS, 15 November 2026
entries.summary: La Poste confirmed to AFP on 14 November that a mid-September attack on its subsidiary Maileva stole the names and postal addresses of 22 million recipients of client companies' mail. Recipients' bank details were not affected, but business clients' IBANs were in a separate billing data set; CNIL was notified, a criminal complaint filed, and the Paris prosecutor opened an investigation on 15 November.
entries.type: Major breach — postal group with banking arm
entries.unknown: Which client companies' recipients are affected; whether letter contents beyond names and postal addresses were consulted — Hôpital Foch says payment-reminder contents may have been; whether the business-client IBANs in the OpenCell billing data were accessed; the intrusion vector and whether any actor has claimed responsibility — reporting does not establish attribution.

entries.bfsi_impact: Banks and financial firms — especially in South Korea and the other countries on the list — should check PHP versions and patch PHP2Shell, and hunt for the scouting activity Cyfirma describes. The report links the actively exploited PHP2Shell flaw to a financially motivated North Korea-linked actor explicitly targeting banks, so PHP-based internet-facing servers are the exposure to close first.
entries.headline: Cyfirma: Lazarus probing PHP2Shell against Korean banks and financial institutions
entries.known: Threat-intelligence firm Cyfirma said in an updated report on PHP2Shell exploitation, published 15 November 2026, that Lazarus — a hacking group believed to be linked to North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau — scouted PHP-based web servers for attack. Dark-web chats in the report show the hackers scouting targets on 27 October, saying some IP ranges in Korea, Japan, the United States, Thailand, Indonesia and India "look promising". The target list Cyfirma obtained contained 216 servers across 10 countries: 30 in South Korea, the fourth most after the United States (49), Japan (47) and India (31). Cyfirma said the hackers prioritised PHP-based web servers in seven sectors — government agencies; banks and financial institutions; telecommunications; critical infrastructure; logistics and aviation; manufacturing; and online trading platforms — and discussed ways to penetrate them, acting with a clear goal of "financial theft and espionage". PHP2Shell lets an attacker take remote control of a server without a password; Cyfirma advised that because the flaw lies in PHP itself rather than in individual websites, updating a site's application alone will not block it.
entries.source_name: Cyfirma report, via Chosun Biz, 15 November 2026 (translated from Korean; English version AI-translated)
entries.summary: Cyfirma said in an updated report on PHP2Shell exploitation published 15 November 2026 that Lazarus scouted PHP-based web servers for attack, with a target list of 216 servers across 10 countries — 30 in South Korea, fourth most after the US, Japan and India. The hackers prioritised servers in seven sectors including banks and financial institutions, with a stated goal of financial theft and espionage. No breach has been confirmed.
entries.type: Ongoing campaign — PHP2Shell targeting of financial sector
entries.unknown: Cyfirma cautioned that appearing on the target list does not mean those servers were actually breached, and said it has not yet confirmed any damage. No victim institution was named, and whether any Korean bank was actually compromised is unconfirmed.

entries.bfsi_impact: South Korea's regulator has found apparent legal violations in the Mirae hacking cases and is widening checks across the sector, so firms with Korean exposure should expect tougher scrutiny of external access points and internal controls; about 580 financial companies and virtual-asset businesses must file first self-check results by 30 November. The finding keeps the Korean AI-driven hacking wave live as a supervisory matter, not just an incident list.
entries.headline: South Korea's FSS finds law violations in Mirae hack probe; orders about 580 financial firms to self-check by 30 November
entries.known: South Korea's Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) has found apparent violations of the Electronic Financial Transactions Act and the Credit Information Use and Protection Act in its on-site inspections of Mirae Asset Life Insurance and Mirae Asset Global Investments, following the hacking incidents at four Mirae Asset group affiliates, Korean press reported on 15 November 2026. The FSS has also completed hacking-related on-site inspections of Shinhan Bank and KB Kookmin Bank and is compiling the results. The FSS has sent checklists on external access points and internal control systems to about 580 financial companies, electronic financial businesses and virtual-asset operators, which must submit first self-check results by 30 November; it will hold sector meetings starting with insurance agencies next week. Reported leak scale so far: about 6,800 people at Mirae Asset Life and about 39,000 at Mirae Asset Securities, including employee information.
entries.source_name: Seoul Economic TV (SEN TV), 15 November 2026 (translated from Korean)
entries.summary: South Korea's Financial Supervisory Service has found apparent legal violations in its inspections of Mirae Asset Life Insurance and Mirae Asset Global Investments after the Mirae group hacks, and has ordered about 580 financial companies and virtual-asset businesses to file first self-check results by 30 November.
entries.type: Sector alert — regulator response
entries.unknown: The specific violations found have not been disclosed in detail and remain under further review; the FSS has not published the inspection results for Shinhan Bank and KB Kookmin Bank.

entries.bfsi_impact: A DeFi lending exploit with direct exchange impact: Korean exchanges froze KAVA transfers, so firms with KAVA exposure or customers trading it should check transfer status and watch for phishing or impersonation using the incident. The loss is small next to the Binance theft, and no traditional bank or broker was affected.
entries.headline: Kava Lend exploited; 55.2 million KAVA drained and about $2.1 million sold
entries.known: On 14 November 2026 the price of KAVA fell by about half in two hours. On-chain analysis by Bitquery found two wallets borrowed 55.2 million KAVA from Kava Lend in 127 loans between 04:04 and 05:42 UTC (12:04-13:42 SGT), exploiting a nearly empty BUSD pool whose interest index grew about 243,000 times in three minutes; each loan was then erased by liquidation, leaving the lending pool with 519 coins against 55.3 million before the attack. A third wallet sold 48.4 million KAVA on BNB Chain in 35 minutes for about $2.09 million, and most of the proceeds were moved to Hyperliquid as about 2,190 XMR bought with $1.17 million. The Relay bridge blocked 612,416 USDT, about 29% of the proceeds. The Kava team said on X around midday UTC that it was aware of the sale, that the event stayed inside its lending app and that nobody had created new coins, and paused a bridge; Crypto Briefing reported that Upbit, Bithumb and Coinone halted KAVA transfers the same day. The wallets had rehearsed with small BUSD deposits, loans and withdrawals between 8 and 10 November.
entries.source_name: Bitquery investigation, 14 November 2026; Crypto Briefing, 14 November 2026
entries.summary: Attackers drained 55.2 million KAVA from the Kava Lend lending protocol on 14 November 2026 and sold about 48.4 million of them for roughly $2.1 million; the Kava team acknowledged the sale, paused a bridge, and three Korean exchanges froze KAVA transfers.
entries.type: DeFi lending protocol exploit — crypto financial services
entries.unknown: The team has not yet said how the lending app failed or published its incident report; whether any further funds can be recovered is not yet known.

entries.bfsi_impact: Financial firms running exposed LLM gateways or AI application platforms should check for the listed IOCs and the exploited flaws, and rotate any exposed API keys; crypto exchanges should watch for deepfake KYC attempts. The self-funding loop means stolen keys can sustain further automated attacks, so exposed AI infrastructure is now a credential-theft target in its own right.
entries.headline: Amazon says ARTEX AI agents stole LLM API keys in self-funding credential-theft loop
entries.known: Amazon Threat Intelligence said its MadPot decoy network, configured to present as LLM inference APIs, captured requests from ARTEX agents between 3 October and 5 November 2026 carrying the agents' own operational memory — system prompts, tool histories, knowledge-graph state and campaign records. The principal campaign stole API keys and other credentials for AI models, feeding the stolen keys into the framework's model gateway so the agents could keep running without the operators paying for inference. Targets included LLM gateways (One API, New API, Veloera, Sub2API, LiteLLM) and AI application platforms (Dify, FastGPT, Langflow, RAGFlow, Open WebUI, LobeChat, Ollama), exploited through default master keys, uninitialised installations, anonymous configuration endpoints, authentication bypass via the isCliRequest header, Langflow remote code execution (CVE-2025-3248) and a RAGFlow authentication bypass (CVE-2026-28797). A second campaign used deepfakes to target cryptocurrency exchange KYC verification. Amazon assessed the ARTEX usage and Chinese-nexus attribution with moderate confidence, notified potentially affected AWS customers, and published IOCs including 104.28.225.223 for credential theft and 212.107.28.51 for cryptocurrency fraud.
entries.source_name: Amazon Threat Intelligence (AWS Security Blog), 13 November 2026
entries.summary: Amazon Threat Intelligence said its MadPot decoy network captured ARTEX AI agents running credential-theft campaigns between 3 October and 5 November 2026, stealing LLM API keys to fund further attacks, and a separate deepfake campaign targeting crypto-exchange KYC checks.
entries.type: Vendor research — AI-driven credential theft and KYC fraud campaigns
entries.unknown: Amazon said it did not observe the activity as it happened and could not independently verify the outcomes the agents reported, so the scale of credentials actually stolen and any downstream compromise are not established. The Chinese-nexus attribution is an assessment, not a proven identity of a specific group.

entries.bfsi_impact: The first US law-enforcement advisory on ARTEX raises it from a research curiosity to a mainstream threat for banks and financial firms: the framework targets overlooked peripheral systems — partner and supplier portals, mobile back-ends and legacy services — and compresses the intrusion window to hours. Firms should apply the FLASH mitigations, inventory internet-facing applications including peripheral ones, and check the published IOCs against their telemetry.
entries.headline: FBI issues FLASH advisory on ARTEX AI attack framework; financial services named among targets
entries.known: The FBI released FLASH-20261113-001, 'Threat Overview of ARTEX Autonomous Penetration Testing Framework', dated 13 November 2026 (TLP:CLEAR, via IC3) and first widely reported on 14 November. It says a variety of malicious actors have used ARTEX since at least August 2026 against organisations globally across financial services, government, technology, defence, semiconductor, energy, healthcare, manufacturing, telecommunications and legal sectors. ARTEX, an open-source LLM-driven multi-agent platform written in Go, turns natural-language objectives into machine commands; some intrusions went from initial targeting to privileged access in under three hours. Notable campaigns cited: financially motivated attacks on South Korean financial institutions that exfiltrated personal information from about 67,000 individuals, and a supply-chain compromise affecting ConnectWise Cloud Backup customers that enabled access to more than 2,250 downstream tenants. The developer 'Autumn-27' released ARTEX on GitHub in July 2026 and removed the repository on 8 October 2026, but forks, localised variants, archived copies and a commercial ARTEX PRO version keep it available; researchers found over 1,600 publicly exposed ARTEX consoles in early November 2026. The FLASH maps observed activity to MITRE ATT&CK, lists mitigations and publishes IOCs including the ARTEX host 38.244.50.120 and the LLM API reseller domain xcai.pro, and asks organisations to vet IOCs before blocking.
entries.source_name: FBI FLASH-20261113-001 via IC3, 13 November 2026
entries.summary: The FBI released FLASH-20261113-001 on 13 November 2026 warning that the ARTEX autonomous penetration-testing framework has been weaponised since at least August 2026 to automate intrusions at machine speed, naming financial services among the targeted sectors and publishing TTPs and IOCs.
entries.type: FBI advisory — AI-driven attack framework
entries.unknown: The FLASH does not name a country behind ARTEX activity; its footnotes cite a Microsoft report on the ConnectWise campaign. The full victim set and the number of financial-services organisations affected are not stated.

entries.bfsi_impact: Treat as an unverified claim with weak evidence: the sample's make-up argues against a genuine brokerage breach, so the immediate risk is phishing using the contact lists rather than account takeover. The posted sample reportedly consists largely of free webmail addresses and includes non-Singaporean contacts, characteristics the reporting notes could indicate an aggregated marketing database rather than a genuine customer database obtained by compromising Webull systems. Webull has not confirmed a security incident and the actor provided no verifiable intrusion details.
entries.source_name: Undercode News, 14 November 2026
entries.summary: A threat actor on a dark-web forum claimed on 14 November 2026 to hold more than 2 million records attributed to Webull Singapore, marketed as 'fresh 2026' data; Webull has not confirmed a security incident and the posted sample looks like aggregated marketing data rather than a genuine customer database.

entries.bfsi_impact: A state-run payment platform for local-currency vouchers has leaked account numbers and encrypted card numbers alongside names and contact details for 3,083 users. The scale is small and the card numbers were encrypted, but account numbers plus personal details are usable for targeted phishing and impersonation of the chak platform and its partner merchants; firms with Korean exposure should watch for fraud attempts citing the platform.
entries.headline: Korea Minting and Security Printing Corporation confirms breach of chak local-currency app; data of 3,083 users leaked
entries.known: The Korea Minting and Security Printing Corporation (KOMSCO) said on 14 November 2026 that unauthorised access to its mobile local-currency platform 'chak' exposed personal data of 3,083 users. Abnormal access was first detected at about 09:30 on 13 November; investigation found an unauthorised party had accessed the system and viewed some personal data. As of 06:00 on 14 November, the confirmed exposed data included names, dates of birth, mobile phone numbers, account numbers, linkage information (CI), email addresses and encrypted card numbers. For 3,072 of the 3,083 people, at most two data items were exposed; 11 people had three to four items exposed. KOMSCO blocked the suspected attack IP, restricted all overseas IP access, temporarily suspended the affected server's service and resumed normal operation after emergency security measures. It reported the incident to the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) and other authorities and is notifying affected customers.
entries.source_name: Hankyung, 14 November 2026 (translated from Korean); Energy Economy, 14 November 2026 (translated from Korean)
entries.summary: South Korea's mint operator KOMSCO said on 14 November 2026 that unauthorised access to its chak local-currency payment app exposed personal data of 3,083 users, including account numbers and encrypted card numbers. The intrusion was detected on 13 November and reported to KISA.
entries.type: Named BFSI victim — data breach
entries.unknown: The attacker and the entry route have not been disclosed. Whether the exposed data has been misused is not yet known.

entries.headline: Threat actor claims full database leak of Honduran payment platform TodoPago; claim unverified
entries.known: A threat actor published a dark-web forum listing claiming to have breached TodoPago, a digital payments platform and payment gateway operating in Honduras, and offering its alleged entire database for free, according to Dark Web Intelligence reporting cited on 14 November 2026. Samples shared with the listing reportedly contain customer names, national identification numbers, email addresses, phone numbers and residential addresses; account numbers and transaction records; merchant records; and BIN information, digital wallet details and point-of-sale information. No verified record count, database size, extraction details or initial access method has been disclosed, and the samples have not been independently authenticated. TodoPago has not publicly confirmed a breach.
entries.source_name: Undercode News, 14 November 2026 (Dark Web Intelligence via X)
entries.summary: A threat actor claims to have leaked the full database of Honduran digital payments platform TodoPago on a dark-web forum, offering it for free. Samples reportedly include national IDs, account numbers, transaction records and merchant data. The claim is unverified and TodoPago has not confirmed a breach.
entries.type: Unverified breach claim — payment platform
